title: Which data streaming platform fits you?

questions.hint: Self-run open-source projects have no licence fee, but your team runs them.

options.label: Our own team
options.why: you have people who can run it

options.label: A vendor
options.why: you want a vendor to run it

options.label: Our cloud provider
options.why: you want your cloud's own service

options.label: All on AWS
options.why: you are all-in on AWS, and Event Hubs and Pub/Sub are run by Microsoft and Google

options.label: All on Azure
options.why: you build on Azure, and MSK, Kinesis and Pub/Sub are run by AWS and Google

options.label: All on Google Cloud
options.why: your apps run on Google Cloud, and MSK, Kinesis and Event Hubs are run by AWS and Microsoft

options.label: More than one cloud
options.why: MSK, Kinesis, Event Hubs and Pub/Sub are each run by one cloud provider

options.label: Data must stay in our own account
options.why: these keep data in your own account or network

questions.q: What does your code speak today?

options.label: The Kafka API already
options.why: these say they support the Kafka API, so your code can often stay as it is

options.label: Nothing yet, it is a new project
options.why: a new project has no Kafka code to move

questions.q: How long must events stay replayable?

options.label: Many months
options.why: Pub/Sub keeps topic messages 31 days at most

questions.hint: Already have Kafka topics? OLake Go, our open-source tool, reads them into Iceberg or Parquet (see the OLake Go section).

options.label: Database changes and streaming from one vendor
options.why: Striim's docs describe change capture and streaming in one product

options.label: Topics that should land as Iceberg tables
options.why: these platforms say they can write Iceberg tables, with limits

options.label: Many teams sharing one setup, in several regions
options.why: Pulsar's docs list multi-tenancy and geo-replication as built-in features

kafka.name: Apache Kafka
kafka.summary: The open-source project whose API most of the platforms here say they support, with no licence fee.
kafka.bestWhen: You have people who can run it and want an open-source project with no licence fee.
kafka.watchOut: Your team owns upgrades, sizing and failures, and Kafka's intro page describes Kafka Connect, not the brokers, as the part that imports data from databases, with no Iceberg writer.

confluent.name: Confluent Cloud
confluent.summary: Fully managed Kafka with 120+ pre-built connectors, on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.
confluent.bestWhen: You want Kafka plus connectors and no servers to run.
confluent.watchOut: The bill has many moving parts: cluster, network, storage, connectors and Flink.

msk.name: Amazon MSK
msk.summary: AWS says it runs open-source Kafka for you.
msk.bestWhen: You are on AWS and already use Kafka.
msk.watchOut: It is an AWS service, and in Provisioned mode you still pick broker types and counts.

warpstream.name: WarpStream
warpstream.summary: Described by WarpStream as a drop-in Kafka replacement built on object storage, with data kept in your own cloud account.
warpstream.bestWhen: Keeping data in a bucket in your own account matters to you.
warpstream.watchOut: Its Tableflow docs say it currently supports append-only tables.

kinesis.name: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
kinesis.summary: AWS's fully managed, serverless streaming service, according to AWS.
kinesis.bestWhen: All your producers and readers live on AWS and the project is new.
kinesis.watchOut: The Kinesis pages we read do not mention Kafka API support, and AWS says it is not currently in the AWS Free Tier.

eventhubs.name: Azure Event Hubs
eventhubs.summary: Microsoft's managed streaming service, with a Kafka endpoint for Kafka clients.
eventhubs.watchOut: The Kafka endpoint needs Standard or higher, and delivery is at least once, so your code must cope with repeats.

pubsub.name: Google Cloud Pub/Sub
pubsub.summary: Google's messaging service, with per-use billing and no servers or capacity to set.
pubsub.bestWhen: Your apps run on Google Cloud and you want simple messaging.
pubsub.watchOut: Topic messages are kept 31 days at most when retention is on, and the pages we read do not mention Kafka protocol support, so expect code changes.

striim.name: Striim
striim.summary: Real-time integration and streaming; its docs describe change capture readers for Oracle, PostgreSQL and SQL Server.
striim.bestWhen: You want change capture and streaming from one vendor.
striim.watchOut: It publishes no open-source licence, the price is not published for Cloud or Platform, and its Iceberg Writer docs name Google Cloud Storage as the only data lake.

redpanda.name: Redpanda
redpanda.summary: Kafka API in a single binary, run by you or by Redpanda, according to its docs.
redpanda.bestWhen: You want Kafka-style code on a different engine, or a self-managed route.
redpanda.watchOut: Iceberg topics need an enterprise licence, and the free Community Edition is source-available, not Apache 2.0.

pulsar.name: Apache Pulsar
pulsar.summary: Open-source messaging whose docs list multi-tenancy and geo-replication as built-in features.
pulsar.bestWhen: Its multi-tenant design fits and you can run it yourself.
pulsar.watchOut: You run it yourself, and the Pulsar docs we read do not state Kafka protocol compatibility.
